title: Cobalt Systems — Onramp & Region Restrictions Discovery
summary: Initial discovery for Redwood Private onramp. Customer's top concerns: strict data residency across EU/UK and APAC regions, limitations on peering to their existing transit fabrics, preference for private endpoints over public IPs, KMS/HSM integration for key control, and detailed egress & audit requirements. Agreement to share Redwood security pack, proposed network diagram, and to run a 1-week pilot (throughput + latency benchmarks) in eu-west-1 and ap-southeast-1.
topics: VPC peering vs transit gateway options
Audit logs, retention and SOC2 concerns
Pilot scope: throughput, latency, and stability tests
Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. I'm Maya, account exec on the Redwood side, and Diego is our systems engineer. Quick intros?
[00:12] Aisha Khan: Hi, I'm Aisha, VP infra at Cobalt Systems. We run a multi-region platform mainly in eu-west-1 and ap-southeast-1, some presence in us-west-2.
[00:20] Tom Becker: Tom, network eng, I look after peering and transit.
[00:24] Priya Patel: Priya, security architect – data residency and KMS questions mostly from me.
[00:29] Diego Ramos: Great, thanks. Quick framing: we assume you're evaluating Redwood Private for production inference, want to understand how we connect into your VPCs, region support, and controls.
[00:38] Aisha Khan: Yup. Topline constraints: EU and UK workloads must stay in-region for certain regulated customers; APAC has additional latency SLOs. We also have a central transit hub in each region and prefer no public egress for inference traffic.
[00:52] Tom Becker: We typically use transit gateways for cross-account routing and prefer AWS PrivateLink / Interface endpoints for SaaS integrations. Peering is only allowed with approved vendors.
[01:03] Diego Ramos: Understood. For Redwood Private we have two common patterns: (1) Private Endpoints (our recommended pattern) using interface endpoints/PrivateLink from customer VPCs to Redwood-managed endpoints; (2) Transit peering where we peer a customer VPC to a Redwood VPC over an AWS Transit Gateway or direct VPC peering in select regions. Both can be configured per-region.
[01:26] Priya Patel: PrivateLink is ideal from a security perspective. How do you handle egress and DNS?
[01:32] Maya Chen: We can route model traffic entirely over private connectivity. DNS is handled via delegated zones or via conditional forwarding — Diego do you want to add details?
[01:39] Diego Ramos: Sure, brief: with PrivateLink we give you an interface endpoint in your VPC and we terminate in Redwood Private's subnet. Traffic never hits the public internet. For DNS, customers can configure private hosted zones or use AWS Route53 resolver rules. We also offer VPC peering with IP-level routing if Transit Gateway policies are a blocker. There are tradeoffs: peering is simpler but scale and routing isolation differ.
[02:02] Tom Becker: Two follow-ups: (a) Do you require BGP / NAT on your side? (b) What about cross-region requests — do we have to replicate endpoints or can you do routing?
[02:13] Diego Ramos: We don't require BGP; connections are standard AWS constructs. For cross-region, best practice is to deploy Redwood Private in the same region as your workload to meet residency and latency. We can route cross-region but that adds latency and egress complexity.
[02:25] Aisha Khan: So we'd prefer eu-west-1 for EU customers and ap-southeast-1 for APAC. Can Redwood support having private deployments in both?
[02:32] Maya Chen: Yes — Redwood Private supports multi-region deployments. The control plane can be centralized, with data plane in-region. You'll be able to pin model versions per region. That said, dedicated capacity and on-prem options differ by region availability and sizing.
[02:45] Priya Patel: KMS: we insist on customer-managed keys for any PII or customer data being cached. Do you integrate with customer KMS or HSM?
[02:54] Diego Ramos: We support customer KMS integration in Private deployments. For HSM-level custody we have partners for HSM-backed key wraps; we'd need to surface requirements and run a security review. Note: some low-level model caches (KV cache) may be encrypted at rest with keys we manage unless customer keys are specified in the config.
[03:12] Priya Patel: Okay, need clarity on which caches use customer keys vs platform keys — we'll list the scope.
[03:17] Tom Becker: Egress: our security policy blocks any unknown external IP ranges. If Redwood needs to reach out for queued downloads or S3 pulls how is that handled?
[03:26] Diego Ramos: For Private deployments you can give us access to your S3 via VPC endpoints or we can use interface endpoints to access customer-owned S3 endpoints. The goal is no public egress. For model downloads during onboarding, we can do initial seed via secured internal transfer or you can provide an internal bucket accessible from the Redwood VPC.
[03:43] Aisha Khan: What about audit logs and retention? We need 7 years for certain customer logs and fine-grained request traces for compliance.
[03:50] Maya Chen: We produce request-level audit logs for Private with configurable retention. Default retention is 1 year in the platform, but for enterprise contracts we support custom retention and export to your logging stack via Kinesis or S3. We'll share the specifics in the security pack.
[04:02] Priya Patel: Good. Also, does Redwood support SAML/SSO with Okta and role-based access control?
[04:07] Diego Ramos: Yes, SAML with Okta is standard; we also support SCIM for provisioning and fine-grained RBAC via roles scoped to models and endpoints.
[04:15] Tom Becker: Network level: any restrictions on CIDR ranges we can peer with? We use /16s internally and have overlapping IP space in some regions.
[04:23] Diego Ramos: Overlapping CIDRs are the main blocker for VPC peering; PrivateLink doesn't require unique CIDRs. If you have overlap we recommend PrivateLink or use a Transit Gateway with route translation. We can support NATing if needed but prefer avoiding complex NAT rules.
[04:41] Aisha Khan: Cost consideration: we have a narrow unit-cost target. Hosted is cheaper to get started but concerns about data leaving region. Dedicated gives cost predictability but still involves shared routing. How should we think about tradeoffs?
[04:54] Maya Chen: Hosted is best for rapid proof-of-value; in cases where data residency or strict isolation matters, Redwood Private is the path. Dedicated is reserved capacity in our hosted region — good for throughput guarantees without setting up private network links. We'll help model TCO: tokens per second, GPU pool costs, egress charges, and PrivateLink / TGW link costs.
[05:10] Priya Patel: For compliance sign-off, we need SOC2 Type II report, ISO attestation, and pen test results.
[05:16] Maya Chen: We'll attach our SOC2 and ISO docs. We also publish a summary of recent penetration tests; full pentest reports may require an NDA.
[05:24] Tom Becker: From a connectivity perspective, what's the usual timeline to stand up a PrivateLink endpoint and test? We have procurement cycles but want an estimate.
[05:32] Diego Ramos: Once contracts are in flight, network setup is usually 2-4 business days for an interface endpoint in a single region, less if you provide the network team with our terraform module. If you want multi-region and routing changes with TGW, plan 1-2 weeks including joint runbook and firewall approvals.
[05:50] Aisha Khan: Ok that aligns with our timeline. We want a pilot in next 30-45 days. Pilot scope: 1) throughput profile with batch sizes, 2) latency SLOs under 95th percentile threshold, 3) correctness regressions on our eval prompts.
[06:05] Maya Chen: Sounds good. We'll propose a pilot plan. For throughput testing we can run in-region eu-west-1 and ap-southeast-1 simultaneously if needed. Diego, do we need any special infra for benchmarking?
[06:14] Diego Ramos: We'll drop a lightweight runner into your VPC or you can run in your app cluster hitting the private endpoint. We capture per-token latency, GPU utilization, and KV cache hit rates. For meaningful numbers, we ask for representative prompt sets and traffic shape.
[06:28] Priya Patel: A note: any PII must be obfuscated in those prompts unless we have the customer-managed key in place for full encryption.
[06:35] Maya Chen: Understood. We'll redact or work with customer KMS.
[06:39] Tom Becker: A few operational questions: Do we have healthchecks, graceful fallback if nodes go down, and a way to route to a backup region?
[06:46] Diego Ramos: We publish health endpoints and support canary/fallback policies; customers can configure per-route fallback to a warm replica region. But again, cross-region fallback will have latency implications and possibly violate residency; it's purely optional and configurable per endpoint.
[07:01] Aisha Khan: Good to know. Let's talk about minimum throughput for dedicated pools — if we need a consistent 100 rps at 512-token averages, what's the ask?
[07:09] Diego Ramos: We'll sketch capacity sizing in the pilot proposal. Roughly—depending on model family and quant, a single GPU instance can handle X tokens/s; we'll provide detailed profiles. For Dedicated you commit to a pool size monthly. For Redwood Private you can provision similar pools inside your VPC.
[07:24] Tom Becker: Any constraints on our side for TLS mutual auth or do you rely on standard TLS?
[07:29] Diego Ramos: Standard TLS is the default; mTLS can be enabled for enhanced mutual auth in Private deployments. That requires cert distribution — we support that via your PKI or our cert manager if approved.
[07:41] Priya Patel: We have a final question on forensic timeline: upon a request, how quickly can you provide per-request metadata for a single customer?
[07:48] Maya Chen: We can provide per-request logs within 24 hours typically, subject to access controls. We also support continuous export if you prefer ingest into your SIEM.
[07:57] Aisha Khan: Okay — next steps?
[08:00] Maya Chen: I'll summarize but Diego will follow up with a technical appendix.
[08:04] Diego Ramos: Action items from our side: share network terraform module, security pack, and a proposed pilot runbook. We'll also include per-region capacity profiles and sample benchmarks.
[08:15] Tom Becker: From Cobalt: we'll share CIDR ranges for our VPCs, existing TGW config, and a redacted prompt set for benchmarking.
[08:23] Priya Patel: And security will send a list of compliance evidence requirements — timelines for ID and any NDA needed.
[08:30] Maya Chen: Great. Anything else?
[08:33] Aisha Khan: One last minor thing: data residency in the UK specifically — some contracts require UK-only storage even though the EU covers most. Are there any special steps for eu-west-2?
[08:44] Diego Ramos: We support deployments in eu-west-2 (London). There are a few extra hoops for capacity there; we'll include region availability notes.
[08:53] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone. We'll capture the notes and send a follow-up with timelines by EOD tomorrow.
[08:58] Aisha Khan: Thanks, bye.
[09:00] End of recording.
